boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's engagement at Dürnstein (11 November 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the attack of Kutusow's Russian army, with the Austrian FML Schmidt, on Marshal Mortier's corps on the left bank of the Danube, from Miloradovitch's morning attack at Loiben to the evening fight with Doktorow's column, the break-through of Gazan's division and Dupont's fight between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein. Mortier's march down the left bank on 10 November and the Russian withdrawal to Krems in the night are context, as are the 6th corps' return of 4 brumaire and Moriggl's order of battle at the Rhine crossing. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Russian and Austrian) under General Kutusow 25,000 men and side A (French) under Marshal Mortier 8,000. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed table, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several, and the passages read do not show his basis. For side B, Alombert and Colin give the three attacking columns 9,000, 2,600 and 3,200 men and put at least 16,000 men, with Essen's reinforcement, against Gazan's division, while Essen and Bagration held the rest of the Russian army in reserve (claim alombert-side-b). Schönhals gives Kutusow's forces as 32,000 men after the sixth Russian column, 7000 strong, joined him at Hollabrunn on the 12th (claim schoenhals-figures); 32,000 less 7000 is 25,000 (our arithmetic), Bodart's figure, but the passages read do not show that Bodart reckoned so. For side A, Alombert and Colin give Gazan's division 5,300 men (claim alombert-side-a) and no strength for Dupont's division, which fought in the evening (claim dupont-division); 8,000 is in none of the passages read. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the table: '1805 11/11. engagement at Dürnstein (3.)'; 'Russians and Austrians | French'; 'Gen. Kutusow | Marshal Mortier'; 'forces: 25,000 | - | 8,000'.

claims.value: Side B (Russian), Alombert and Colin's figures: General Doktorow, with 16 battalions and 2 squadrons, 9,000 men, was to move by Egelsee and Scheibenhof on Weissenkirchen to take Gazan's column in the rear; General Stryck, with 5 battalions, 2,600 men, was to move by Egelsee onto the French left flank; and Miloradovitch, with 7 battalions and 2 squadrons, 3,200 men, was to attack Mortier's troops in front and throw them back into the defile. General Essen II at Stein and Bagration beyond Krems held the rest of the Russian army in reserve. With the reinforcement Essen gave Miloradovitch for his second attack, at least 16,000 men were to assail the 5,300 men of Gazan's division. Their footnotes give the units of the three columns, citing Danilewski for the first.
claims.rationale: Side A's official history, read from the page images; the figures are its reconstruction, and it cites Danilewski's Russian relation for the first column's units. The three columns make 14,800 men (our sum); the passages read give no figure for Essen's reinforcement, which brings the total to at least 16,000. Bodart's 25,000 (claim bodart-strength) differs, and the passages read do not show whether it counts the reserves under Essen and Bagration. Schönhals gives the turning force, after Kotzebue, as 10,000 (claim schoenhals-figures). Kutusow, on the Austrian General Schmidt's advice, resolved to carry off Gazan's division and assigned these columns to the attack (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Side A (French), Alombert and Colin's figures: Gazan's division had 5,300 men. In their narrative (OCR), Mortier hastened on with Gazan's division alone, the other divisions being too far off; at Weideneck he found boats enough to carry the 4e léger and the 100e de ligne with artillery, which landed at Weissenkirchen, and the 103e went on to bivouac by the road between Wadstein and Dürrenstein. In their reckoning of the losses, the 4e léger had put 1,500 men in line on 11 November, and the 100e and the 103e had 1,300 and 1,600 men in the ranks on 22 November 'out of 2,000 present on the 11th'; no strength is given for the 4e dragons.
claims.rationale: Side A's own official history: the 5,300 is read from the page image of p. 143 and the regiments' strengths from p. 166, and the march is read in the OCR. We read the 2,000 as each regiment's, since 1,300 and 1,600 together exceed it; read so, the three infantry regiments put 5,500 men in line (our sum), against the 5,300 given for the division on p. 143, and the passages read do not reconcile the two. The narrative's counts of the French troops engaged at stages of the morning are read only in the OCR and are not restated (open questions). Dupont's division, which fought in the evening, is a separate claim (dupont-division). Gazan's division was on the field from the evening before by the earlier movement, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): as in claim alombert-side-b for the 5,300; 'Mortier therefore hastens, but with Gazan's division alone, the ... (OCR) others being too far away' (OCR); 'having reached Weideneck, opposite Melk, he finds there boats in sufficient number to carry the 4e léger and the 100e de ligne, with ... (OCR) pieces of artillery' (OCR); 'the whole is landed at Weissenkirchen' (OCR); 'the 103e rejoins the artillery at Weissenkirchen, passes it, and goes to bivouac by the road between Wadstein and Dürrenstein' (OCR); 'of all the corps engaged in the combat of Dürrenstein, the one that suffered most was the 4e léger. In its return of 22 November it reports 728 prisoners; it has 155 men in hospital; it has barely 500 left in the ranks, instead of the 1,500 it had put in line on 11 November'; 'the 100e and the 103e had suffered less. Each of them had left 160 to 170 prisoners in the enemy's hands and sent 320 men to hospital. There remained to the one 1,300, to the other 1,600 men in the ranks on 22 November, out of 2,000 present on the 11th'.

claims.value: Schönhals's figures, from the Austrian side: the column of Doctorow's division and Maltiz's brigade, which FML Schmidt led himself, was to turn the French; Schmidt left two battalions on the ridge and one in the valley and advanced on Dürrenstein with the rest, and the Russians, about 500 men strong, formed up outside Dürrenstein. The French made front against them on a gentle spur between the Danube and the vineyards with two guns, and their cavalry, about 400 horses, stood before Loiben. By his footnote, Kotzebue has 10,000 Russians intended for turning the French reach Egelsee in four columns, with two guns brought along with difficulty. In the OCR, Kutusow had drawn up his army at Krems, Bagration camped at Stratzing with a number of battalions and Miloradovic's division held Stein. Kutusow's forces grew to 32,000 men by his union with his sixth column, which arrived 7000 strong at Hollabrunn on the 12th. Schönhals gives no total for either side at Dürrenstein.
claims.rationale: Side B's own side's account, read from the page images except where marked OCR. Schönhals gives no count for Miloradović's division or for the whole column. Where he has the Russians, about 500 men strong, form up outside Dürrenstein, the Austrian relation that Alombert and Colin quote (claim side-b-losses-reported) has the column deploy about ... (OCR) paces from the town, and their narrative has Doktorow's advanced guard deploy ... (OCR) paces east of Dürrenstein (OCR); the passages read do not show which the relation's original gives. His two guns and about 400 horses for the French stand in that relation as quoted (OCR). Kotzebue's 10,000, which Schönhals reports at second hand, is the turning force only. Schönhals's footnote says that, for want of more reliable sources, some details were taken from Kotzebue's description of the engagement; Alombert and Colin hold that the later German relations all rest mainly, almost solely, on Kotzebue's work, and that he had not been present at the combat (OCR). Bodart's 25,000 (claim bodart-strength) equals the 32,000 less the 7000 of the sixth column (our arithmetic); the passages read do not show that Bodart reckoned so. The claim mixes forces that Kutusow's plan assigned to the attack, side A's troops on the field and the army's strength after the engagement, so it is tagged unresolved. claims.value: Side A (French), Dupont's division, which fought in the evening: in Alombert and Colin (OCR), Dupont had stopped at Marbach by their account of the day before the engagement, and then set his division in bivouac between Spitz and Weissenkirchen, ordering the 1st hussars and the 9e léger to Weissenkirchen and placing the 32e between Weissenkirchen and Spitz and the 96e at Spitz. Dupont's troops, marching to Gazan's help, fought the greater part of Doktorow's column between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein: first the 9e, then the 32e, which Dupont brought up to relieve it, while the 96e stood in reserve at Weissenkirchen. The return of the troops present under arms in the 6th corps on 4 brumaire, which Alombert and Colin print, records its 1st division, the 9e léger, the 32e and the 96e, as detached with Prince Murat and gives it no figures, and records the 1st hussars as detached to the 1st division. Moriggl gives Dupont's division, the 9th light and the 32nd and 96th line infantry under the brigadiers Rouyer and Marchand, 7 battalions and 5350 men at the Grande Armée's crossing of the Rhine.
claims.rationale: The march and the fight are read in the OCR of Alombert and Colin's narrative, which quotes Talandier's relation and an account of Dupont's fight that it does not name in the passages read; the regiment numbers are those printed on the page image of p. 769, and the return's date, 4 brumaire an XIV, is 26 October 1805 by our conversion. The targeted follow-up for side A's strength: the 6th corps' return gives no figures for Dupont's division, which was detached, and Moriggl's order of battle, an Austrian and Tyrolean account with French strengths at second hand, gives 5350 men at the start of the campaign, before the division's fight at Haslach (entry B363c). Neither gives its strength on 11 November, and no passage read gives the strength of the troops it engaged. Dupont's division was on the march behind Gazan's before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited; Dupont's own orders that evening are recorded in claim side-a-command. (OCR) leagues ahead of Spitz, at Weissenkirchen"' (OCR); 'he places the 32nd between Weissenkirchen and Spitz, and the 96th in the latter village' (OCR); '[at ... claims.value: Kutusow commanded side B and decided the attack. In Alombert and Colin, informed on the evening of the 10th by marauders taken by the Russians that Gazan's division was isolated, he resolved, on the advice of the Austrian General Schmidt, who acted as chief of staff, to carry off Gazan's division, and as he believed its bulk to be in the defile between Weissenkirchen and Dürnstein he meant to crush it there; Doktorow, Stryck and Miloradovitch led the three columns, with Essen II and Bagration in reserve. Doktorow's column reached Egelsee only after noon, and Schmidt, who went with it, thinking that Mortier had passed Dürnstein, had it bear left and come down into the valley toward Dürnstein and Wadstein. In their narrative (OCR), Doktorow, learning on the way down that Dupont's division was near Weissenkirchen, turned against this new adversary to contain it so that Miloradovitch and Schmidt could carry through their joint action against Gazan's division. In their judgment the only combatant of 11 November who fell short of his task was General Dokhtourow, whose slowness made Schmidt's plan fail. In Schönhals, Kutusow decided on the evening of the 10th to attack the French the next day, after FML Schmidt's plan: a column was to march early to Egelsee, pass Scheibenhof in silence, gain the ravine of Weissenkirchen and fall on the enemy's rear, while Miloradović's division attacked in front from Stein. The column, which Schmidt led himself, was so delayed that it left Egelsee only in the afternoon; to keep to the plan Schmidt brought its bulk down to the Danube through a ravine between Dürrenstein and Weissenkirchen, part of it passing through Dürrenstein as Gerhardt's column came down over the ruin, and neither Schmidt nor other officers could bring the Russians, who feared the columns' separation, to leave a garrison in the little town.
claims.rationale: Both accounts read from the page images, except the OCR where marked. They agree that Kutusow decided the attack and that the Austrian Schmidt advised or planned it and went with the turning column. They differ on the hour the column reached or left Egelsee (Alombert and Colin, there only after noon; Schönhals, leaving only at 1 in the afternoon; Kotzebue in Schönhals's footnote, arriving at 2 in the night) and on its leader: Alombert and Colin name Doktorow's column, which Schmidt accompanied, Schönhals the column Schmidt led himself, with Gerhardt's column beside it. These are the commanders' decisions at the engagement, so the claim is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Marshal Mortier commanded side A on the field, General Gazan his division; Schönhals puts Mortier's corps quarters at Dürrenstein the night before. In Alombert and Colin (OCR), Mortier told Fabvier, as he arrived on the field, to go forward and turn the ground to the best account; resolved to drive the enemy out of Unter-Loiben for good, putting a battalion of the 100e under Major Henriod into line along the Danube and directing companies of the 103e under chef de bataillon Pasquier and General Campana onto the plateau; and, once he saw the troops in bivouac, Gazan having ordered the bivouacs for the night, rode off with an escort to meet Dupont's division, met the Russian column just beyond the town and had to fight his way back to Gazan's division. Facing the concentric attack, he resolved first to gather all his means on the plateau near Ober-Loiben; in the relation they quote, he determined to gather the division's troops in front of the plateau held by a battalion of the 100e, to await the enemy's shock there and, after repelling it, to attempt the retreat. He tried first to overthrow the column, which he did not judge very numerous; then Major Henriod of the 100e proposed to lead his regiment's grenadiers into the walled road by which the enemy was advancing, and the Marshal ordered it carried out at once. Apart from him, General Dupont brought up a regiment to relieve the one engaged and, wishing to make an end, had its colonel pull his men out of the mêlée man by man and rally them (claim dupont-division).

claims.value: Bodart places side B (Russian and Austrian) under General Kutusow in the left column of his table, the winner's place by his stated rule, so he records a victory of side B over side A (French) under Marshal Mortier on 11 November. Alombert and Colin call the affair of Dürrenstein a fine success for Kutusow, although Mortier, with two-thirds of Gazan's division, escaped with glory from the envelopment that threatened him. In Schönhals the advantage of the day was dearly bought with FML Schmidt's death, all the Russian troops withdrew with their prisoners to Krems during the night, and the engagement gained Kutusow time to send his artillery reserve and baggage ahead undisturbed and to prepare his union with Auersperg's corps and the sixth Russian column.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A lost), read from Bodart's table and rule, with the other accounts' ending, read from the page images. No source read gives a different result. In the passages read, Dupont's division bivouacked on the battlefield that evening while Gazan's passed into the second line, by the journal of Dupont's division as Alombert and Colin quote it, and the Russian troops withdrew to Krems in the night (Schönhals); the passages read do not show what Bodart based his result on. English renderings (ours): Bodart, p. 46, 'the winner's place in the comparisons is always to be sought on the left side, the loser's on the right'; the table as in claim bodart-strength; Alombert and Colin, 'although Mortier, with two-thirds of Gazan's division, escaped with glory from the envelopment with which he was threatened, the affair of Dürrenstein was a fine success for Kutusow'; '"in the evening", says the journal of Dupont's division, "the division bivouacs on the battlefield; Gazan's division passes into the second line. The Batavians occupy Spitz"'; Schönhals, 'here FML Schmidt sank, struck by four Russian bullets, by whose death the advantage of the day was dearly bought'; 'all the Russian troops withdrew with their prisoners to Krems during the night'; 'the engagement at Dürrenstein had the result that Kutusow gained time to send ahead, undisturbed, his artillery reserve and the baggage, and also to make the necessary arrangements for his union with Auersperg's corps and the sixth Russian column, which arrived 7000 strong at Hollabrunn on the 12th'.

claims.value: Side A's loss in the other accounts. Alombert and Colin: the 4e léger, the corps that suffered most, reported in its return of 22 November 728 prisoners and 155 men in hospital, and had barely 500 left in the ranks of the 1,500 it had put in line on 11 November; more than 700 of its men were taken, caught, they suppose, between the two Russian columns from Stein and Dürrenstein, while north of the road the 103e had relatively few taken. The 100e and the 103e each left 160 to 170 prisoners and sent 320 men to hospital; the 4e dragons left only 65 prisoners but had barely one man in two unhurt, 123 men still serving on 22 November and 101 in hospital. In sum Gazan's division appears to have lost about 1,600 to 1,700 men, a little more than a third of its strength, of whom 1,100 to 1,200 were prisoners; the Austrian report (XIII-61) gives only 980. The French artillery could not be saved; Lieutenant Fabvier abandoned his pieces on orders, after spiking them. In their narrative (OCR) General Graindorge and others were taken when their boat ran aground near Stein against the bridge piers, the eagles were saved, and the squadron commander Rozat saved the dragoons' guidons. Schönhals: besides a considerable number of dead, the French lost 2000 prisoners, among them the whole 4th Dragoon regiment, 1 general, 3 colonels and 50 officers, and 2 flags and 5 guns, not counting the two guns the Russians had lost in the morning; one boat was sunk at Stein by the Russian artillery and went down with 400 men, and another, caught on a bridge pier, was taken with the 300 men aboard; General Gazan escaped from the bloodbath at Dürrenstein with only 400 men and 50 horses.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images except where marked OCR, and not combined. Alombert and Colin's regimental figures come from the returns of 22 November; their summary is an estimate ('parait avoir perdu environ'), and the passages read do not show how it was reached. Its 1,600 to 1,700 is 30 to 32 per cent of the 5,300 given for the division on p. 143, where the text says a little more than a third (our arithmetic). Their 'n'en accuse que 980' follows their count of prisoners, and the passages read do not make plain whether the Austrian report's 980 counts the prisoners or the whole loss. The accounts differ on the prisoners (Alombert and Colin 1,100 to 1,200; the Austrian report 980; Schönhals 2000; Bodart 1,600, claim bodart-losses), on the 4e dragons (Schönhals the whole regiment taken; Alombert and Colin 65 prisoners), on the trophies (Bodart 5 guns and 2 eagles; Schönhals 2 flags and 5 guns; Alombert and Colin the artillery lost and the eagles saved, OCR) and on Gazan's escape (Alombert and Colin two-thirds of the division with Mortier; Schönhals Gazan with only 400 men and 50 horses). The surrender of 1,000 men on the height in the evening is the Austrian relation's (claim side-b-losses-reported), which Alombert and Colin cite for the Allies' belief, held for some time, that only a small detachment of cavalry had escaped (OCR). English renderings (ours): as in claim alombert-side-a for the 4e léger, the 100e and the 103e; 'the 4e léger, caught no doubt between the two Russian columns that came out of Stein and Dürrenstein and joined at Loiben, had more than 700 men taken prisoner'; 'north of the road the situation stayed better. The companies of the 103e (3rd battalion) posted at the important points prolonged the resistance there to the end, and this regiment had relatively few men taken prisoner'; 'the 4e dragons left only 65 prisoners in the enemy's hands; but it had barely one man unhurt in two: 123 men were still doing duty on 22 November, 101 were in hospital'; 'in sum, Gazan's division appears to have lost about 1,600 to 1,700 men, a little more than a third of its strength, of whom 1,100 to 1,200 prisoners'; 'the Austrian report (XIII-61) admits only 980 of them'; as in claim bodart-winner for the two-thirds; 'our artillery could not be saved. Lieutenant Fabvier "defended himself on the plateau until he received the order to abandon his pieces, which he did only after spiking them,"' (p. 162); 'others, among them General Graindorge, were less fortunate' (OCR); 'their boat ran aground near Stein against the piers of the bridge, and they fell into the enemy's hands' (OCR); '[the volleys with which they were pursued killed a few men,] but the eagles were saved' (OCR); 'squadron commander Rozat saved the regiment's guidons' (OCR); 'the Allies remained persuaded that this small detachment of cavalry alone had been able to escape the disaster' (OCR); Schönhals, 'the French losses amounted, besides a considerable number of dead, to 2000 prisoners, among whom were the whole 4th Dragoon regiment, then 1 general, 3 colonels and 50 officers'; 'besides that, 2 flags, 5 guns were taken from them' (pp. 136-137); 'not counting the two guns that the Russians had lost in the morning' (p. 137); 'yet one of them was sunk at Stein by the Russian artillery and went down with 400 men; another got caught on a bridge pier and was taken together with the 300 men embarked on it'; 'General Gazan escaped from the bloodbath at Dürrenstein with only 400 men and 50 horses, over the ruin of Scheibenhof and Ostra toward Spitz'.

claims.value: Side B's loss in the other accounts. Alombert and Colin: the Austrian report (XIII-61) gives the Russians' loss as 920 men, without saying whether it includes wounded and prisoners. An Austrian relation that they quote has the Russians on the road to Dürnstein fire on one another from both sides of the road, FML Schmidt find his death there, and, when the burning of Loiben had lit the basin, the French infantry on the height lay down its arms, 1,000 men, and the two guns lost retaken. In their narrative (OCR), a French charge threw the Russians back into Unter-Loiben in the morning and carried guns, General Campana's companies took further guns and the men defending them, and in the evening, in the account of Dupont's fight, all the Russians not killed or taken threw themselves into the Danube or fled into the mountains. Schönhals: FML Schmidt fell, struck by four Russian bullets, where troops of one and the same power fired on each other; at the height 1000 men laid down their arms, and the two Russian guns lost in the fight were found again.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images except where marked OCR, and not combined. Bodart's 4,000 killed and wounded (claim bodart-losses) differs from the Austrian report's 920 as Alombert and Colin cite it; the passages read give no other count of the Russian loss. Schmidt's death is in all three accounts. The relation's surrender of 1,000 French is reported as an Allied claim: Alombert and Colin have no doubt that the grenadiers broke through, since all the most disinterested French documents mention it (OCR; claim side-a-command). The relation that Alombert and Colin quote begins on p. 161, where the OCR labels it 'KE 46' and the introduction's list of sources names Austrian relations XI-46 and XIII-61 (OCR); Schönhals's evening follows it nearly sentence for sentence (open questions). claims.value: Alombert and Colin: above Dürnstein the Danube washes the foot of the mountains on its left bank; between Dürnstein and Rothenhof it moves away from them around the small alluvial plain on which the villages of Ober- and Unter-Loiben stand, and from Rothenhof to Stein it again runs along the foot of the escarpments, leaving barely room for the road. The spurs of the mountain end in vine-covered slopes; one runs out into a small flat, rectangular plateau with steep edges north-east of Unter-Loiben, and another plateau ends above the road over Ober-Loiben. In their narrative (OCR) snow covered the ground the night before; the ground was broken and covered with vines and walls, so that the infantry and dragoons left in reserve could not be used there; a dragoon officer found vines, ditches and walls everywhere, obstacle upon obstacle; and in the evening the Russian column came along a walled road. The Austrian relation they quote calls the road to Dürnstein an embanked road bordered by walls, as often in wine country. Schönhals (OCR): the whole left bank of the Danube from Grein, above all from Weissenkirchen to Krems, is very steep and cut by ravines; at Dürrenstein a castle ruin on the rock is joined by a wall to the little town, through which the road runs; at Loiben a small plain covered with vineyards lies between the foot of the mountains and the Danube, and the road to Stein across it is bounded by a wall on each side. In his narrative (page images) the French, by holding the slopes with guns, could inflict heavy losses on those advancing in the plain; Schmidt's column came down to the Danube through a ravine between Dürrenstein and Weissenkirchen; and Dürrenstein is the little town that blocks the pass.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images except where marked OCR. Alombert and Colin set Kotzebue's account aside for the fighting but use it, with every reserve, for the positions before the engagement and those of the artillery, on which his informants could know more and which do not disagree with the trustworthy Russian and French documents (open questions). The vineyard walls, the walls of the road to Dürnstein and the castle ruin are recorded here as ground; claim fortification records why they are not coded as works. The ground stood before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'we think we should set this little work wholly aside for everything that concerns the fighting'; 'it seems that, for the positions held before the engagement and for those of the artillery, the inhabitants may have informed Kotzebue with more competence'; 'this part of their accounts, moreover, is not, like the rest, in disagreement with the trustworthy Russian and French documents, so that we think we may make use of it, with every reserve'; 'the Danube, above Dürnstein, washes the foot of the mountains on its left bank'; 'between Dürnstein and Rothenhof it moves away from them, going round the small alluvial plain on which the villages of Ober- and Unter-Loiben were built; from Rothenhof to Stein it again runs along the foot of the escarpments, leaving barely the space needed for the road'; 'the spurs of the mountain die away roughly on that line, and they end in slopes covered with vines'; 'one of these spurs runs out into a small plateau with a horizontal surface, rectangular in shape, with steep edges, north-east of Unter-Loiben'; 'another plateau, of similar shape, ends above the road, plumb over Ober-Loiben'; '"snow covered the ground", says Colonel Talandier; "the cold was piercing"' (OCR); 'there still remained in reserve ... (OCR)' (OCR) '... of the ... (OCR) and the ... (OCR) dragoons, which could not be used in this broken ground, covered with vines and walls' (OCR); '"everywhere vines, ditches, walls, obstacle upon obstacle", says an officer of dragoons' (OCR); as in claim side-a-command for the walled road (OCR); the relation, as in claim side-b-losses-reported for the road (p. 162); Schönhals, 'the whole left bank of the Danube from Grein, but above all from Weissenkirchen to Krems, is very steep and cut through with ravines' (p. 133, OCR); '[at Dürrenstein steep rock walls rise,] on whose summit lies a castle ruin, which is connected by a wall with the little town, through which the road leads' (p. 134, OCR); 'at the village of Loiben a small plain covered with vineyards forms between the feet of the mountains and the Danube, through which the road runs toward Stein, which, as is usually the case in vine country, is bounded left and right by a wall' (OCR); 'the French, however, by occupying the slopes with guns, had the great advantage of inflicting great losses on those advancing in the plain' (p. 135); as in claim side-b-command for the ravine and the little town.

claims.value: Both sides attacked. Mortier was preparing to attack on the morning of 11 November when Miloradovitch forestalled him, and the combat fell into two phases, Miloradovitch and Stryck in the morning and Doktorow in the evening. In their narrative (OCR), the Russians suddenly took the offensive and Miloradovitch attacked both in the small plain of Loiben and on the slopes; French light infantry battalions drove the enemy back into the wood, and a French charge threw the Russians back into Unter-Loiben; Mortier resolved to drive them out of Unter-Loiben for good. Danilewski's relation, which they find in close agreement with the French documents, has a French attack on the Russian right fail and Mortier finally drive Miloradovitch out of Loiben and pursue him to Stein; in the plain, therefore, the French success was final, though not in the mountains. In the evening Doktorow's advanced guard, having passed through Dürrenstein, deployed east of the town in a concentric attack on the division; on Mortier's order the grenadiers attacked into the walled road by which it advanced, and the Russian column broke up. Between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein a regiment that Dupont brought up beat the charge against Doktorow's column while the Russians came on with equal daring, and Doktorow, by Danilewski, was forced to clear the road and let Mortier pass.
claims.rationale: Code both_attacked: Alombert and Colin describe main attacks by each side, Miloradovitch's on Loiben, answered by a French offensive that drove him back to Stein, and Doktorow's on Gazan's rear, met by Dupont's attack between Weissenkirchen and Wadstein on another part of the field. The French were bivouacked, not holding a defended position, when they drove Miloradovitch to Stein, so the exception for a counterattack inside a defended position does not apply. Their account rests, by their own list, on French documents (a regimental colonel's letter to Berthier, General Graindorge's report on his artillery, the journal of Dupont's division and the notes in the return of the officers), on two partial Austrian eyewitness relations in the Vienna war archives and on Danilewski's Russian relation, and, with precautions, on Talandier's narrative and Rozat's fragment; there is no official French relation of the combat (OCR). Schönhals's account, coded separately, has only side B attack (claim posture-schoenhals). Both commanders decided to attack at this engagement, Kutusow in resolving to carry off Gazan's division and Mortier in preparing to attack and resolving to clear Unter-Loiben, so the posture is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Side B attacked. Kutusow decided on the evening of the 10th to attack the French the next day; at 7 in the morning Miloradović's division attacked the French advanced posts by the Danube, threw them back and occupied Unter-Loiben; the French, holding the slopes with guns, threw back the Russian right wing, forcing the troops by the Danube into a short backward movement, and not long after Ober-Loiben too was stormed. In the evening Schmidt's column came down behind Dürrenstein; the French made front against it, their cavalry's attempts to break through were repulsed, everyone advanced on the height where the French infantry stood, and 1000 men laid down their arms. In Schönhals's footnote after Kotzebue, Dupont's division ran into Schmidt's column at Wadstein and tried to break through, but, taken in flank and rear, had to re-embark and cross to Rossatz.
claims.rationale: Code B_attacked: Schönhals has side B attack throughout, and side A's repulse of the Russian right wing, its cavalry's attempts to break through and Dupont's attempt in Kotzebue's version are counter-strokes or attempts to escape by the side attacked. Alombert and Colin's account is coded separately (claim posture-alombert-colin). The passage does not say who stormed Ober-Loiben. By his footnote Schönhals took some details from Kotzebue for want of more reliable sources, and his editors call his account of the engagement meagre and incomplete for want of material, pointing to its description in their journal's volume for 1860. Kutusow decided the attack at this engagement, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): as in claim side-b-command for the decision; 'at 7 in the morning Miloradović's division attacked the enemy's advanced posts by the Danube. These were thrown back and Unter-Loiben occupied'; as in claim durnstein-ground for the slopes; 'and in fact they threw the Russians' right wing back again, and this circumstance forced the detachments fighting by the Danube too into a short backward movement; not long after, Ober-Loiben too was stormed'; 'it was 4 in the afternoon when the head of Schmidt's column came down through the ravine to the Danube about 2000 paces behind Dürrenstein'; as in claim schoenhals-figures for the French front; 'the latter at once made an attack in the flat vineyards on the wing leaning on the Danube and tried to cut its way through, but was repulsed by a violent musketry'; 'the Russian Jäger advanced skirmishing on the slope of the mountain, while the column following deployed and kept up the fire until dark, without advancing'; 'the fire of the French grew ever weaker'; as in claims side-b-information and side-b-losses-reported for the evening; footnote, 'according to Kotzebue, Dupont's division ran into FML Schmidt's column at about 4 in the afternoon at the moment when the latter arrived at Wadstein, coming down from Resch'; 'it tried to break through, but, taken in flank and rear, after a bloody hand-to-hand fight it had to re-embark and cross over to Rossatz'; as in claim schoenhals-figures for Kotzebue as a source; '[editors' footnote] the above account of the engagement at Dürrenstein has turned out meagre and incomplete for want of the material available to the author'; 'all the more as it was described in this journal, volume for 1860'.

claims.value: Neither account names works that either side fought from. Side A had passed the night in the basin of Loiben (Alombert and Colin, OCR), its division camped with the right wing at Ober-Loiben and the left on the lower slopes of the heights (Schönhals, OCR), with small posts on the neighbouring heights, which Alombert and Colin give with every reserve from Kotzebue (OCR), and pickets by the ruins of the castle and on the Neudeck (Schönhals). In the fighting side A held the plateaus above the villages, on one of which Fabvier defended his guns, and heights near the castle of Dürnstein (Alombert and Colin). Side B came down from the mountains, part of it through the little town of Dürrenstein, which Schmidt found unoccupied (Schönhals). The walls named are those of the vineyards and of the road to Dürnstein, along which the Russian column advanced in the evening and the grenadiers attacked it (Alombert and Colin, OCR, and the Austrian relation they quote), and the wall that joins the castle ruin above Dürrenstein to the town (Schönhals, OCR).
claims.rationale: none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. The vineyard and road walls are named as obstacles and as the setting of the evening fight, not as works either side fought from, and no passage read has either side defend the castle ruin or the town; if the walls of the road were counted as works, the evening fight on the road would code B_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'our troops had passed the night in the basin of Loiben, in gloomy weather,' (OCR); Schönhals, 'the division camped with its right wing at Ober-Loiben, with its left on the lower, fairly steep slopes of the heights of the same name' (OCR); Alombert and Colin, 'we place small posts on the neighbouring heights, Pfaffenberg, Laken and Neudeck' (OCR); 'this last information with every reserve. It comes from the [attempt at a description of the battle at Dürnstein] of Captain W. von Kotzebue (... (OCR)), a very inexact work,' (OCR); Schönhals, 'by the ruins of the castle and on the ridge of the mountain, the so-called Neudeck, stood pickets, whose patrols came close to the Scheibenhof' (p. 135); Alombert and Colin, as in claim durnstein-ground for the plain and the plateaus; as in claim side-b-losses-reported for General Campana on the plateau (OCR); as in claim side-a-losses-reported for Fabvier on the plateau (p. 162); as in claim side-a-command for the plateau near Ober-Loiben (OCR); '[a regiment that had bivouacked behind Dürrenstein crossed the town ...,] detaching its ... open_questions: Deferred: Alombert's own book on the combat of Dürrenstein, which by t. IV's preface (OCR, read and not cited) prints a great part of the documents of this period and appeared in 1897, and in which the French documents that t. IV quotes are given (Colonel Taupin's letter, Talandier's relation, General Graindorge's and chef de bataillon Lasseront's reports, Rozat's recollections, the journal of Dupont's division and the officers' service notes); it was not inspected, so these are read only as t. IV quotes them. Also deferred: the Austrian relations XI-46 and XIII-61 of the Vienna war archives and Danilewski's Russian relation, known only from t. IV's quotations and summaries; Kotzebue's description of the battle (dated 1807 in t. IV's OCR), known only from Schönhals's footnotes and t. IV's critique; the account of the engagement in the Österreichische militärische Zeitschrift for 1860 to which Schönhals's editors refer; Victoires et conquêtes, t. XV, which t. IV identifies as Talandier's relation or written from his notes (OCR); and the rest of t. IV's introduction for 10 November (pp. 130-137), which opens with Murat's march on Vienna and of which only the first lines and the passages around the names Mortier, Gazan, Kutusow and Dupont were read, none of them cited. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: t. IV's counts of the French troops engaged at stages of the morning and of the reserve left unused, the corps it says the Russians detached toward Weissenkirchen, the strength of Doktorow's advanced guard and of the Russians the hussars saw coming down at Weissenkirchen, the numbers in Major Henriod's harangue and in his service record, the size of the grenadiers' sections and of Mortier's escort, the guns and men General Campana's companies took, the men and horses Rozat saved, the losses of the 9e léger and the 32e in its footnotes, the distances at which the Russian column deployed, Bagration's battalions in Schönhals, and the hours and dates except those printed on the page images; the page numbers of the parents, read from the OCR except where a page image is cited.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. Bodart gives 8,000; Alombert and Colin give Gazan's division 5,300 men (5,500 by their regiments' figures, on our reading) and no strength for Dupont's division, which fought the evening's second action with at least its 9e léger and 32e. The targeted follow-up searched t. IV's appendix of situations for a return of Dupont's division: the 6th corps' return of 4 brumaire an XIV (26 October by our conversion), read from the page image of p. 769, gives none, the division being detached with Prince Murat; Moriggl's order of battle, already registered, gives it 7 battalions and 5350 men at the Rhine crossing (p. 92), a figure from the start of the campaign (claim dupont-division). That leaves the gap open. A return of Dupont's division for November, the journal of the division or Alombert's book, none of which the passages read print in full, could close it. Side B's strength is less open: Alombert and Colin give the three columns, and Bodart's 25,000 equals Schönhals's 32,000 less the sixth column's 7000 (our arithmetic), though the passages read do not show that he reckoned so.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side B's strength (Bodart 25,000; Alombert and Colin at least 16,000 assailing Gazan's division, in columns of 9,000, 2,600 and 3,200 with Essen's reinforcement, the rest of the army in reserve; Kotzebue, through Schönhals, 10,000 for the turning force); side A's strength (Bodart 8,000; Alombert and Colin 5,300 for Gazan's division and no figure for Dupont's); side A's loss (Bodart 6,600, of which 1,600 prisoners; Alombert and Colin about 1,600 to 1,700, of which 1,100 to 1,200 prisoners; the Austrian report XIII-61 980; Schönhals 2000 prisoners besides many dead; the Austrian relation that Alombert and Colin quote, 1,000 men laying down their arms on the height, which Alombert and Colin reject); the 4e dragons (Schönhals the whole regiment taken; Alombert and Colin 65 prisoners); the trophies (Bodart 5 guns and 2 eagles; Schönhals 2 flags and 5 guns; Alombert and Colin the artillery lost and the eagles saved, OCR); Gazan's escape (Alombert and Colin two-thirds of the division with Mortier; Schönhals Gazan with 400 men and 50 horses); Dupont's evening fight (Alombert and Colin, after the account of Dupont's fight that they quote, Danilewski and the journal of Dupont's division, the Russians forced to let Mortier pass and Dupont's division bivouacking on the battlefield; Kotzebue, through Schönhals, Dupont's division re-embarking for Rossatz); side B's loss (Bodart 4,000 killed and wounded; the Austrian report 920); the hours of the turning column (Alombert and Colin, at Egelsee only after noon and down in the valley at 5 o'clock; Schönhals, leaving Egelsee at 1 in the afternoon, its head down at 4; Kotzebue at Egelsee at 2 in the night); who set Loiben on fire (the Austrian relation, the French; Alombert and Colin's narrative and the account of Dupont's fight that they quote, the Russians, OCR); and the posture code (both_attacked from Alombert and Colin, B_attacked from Schönhals).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; the passages read do not show his sources, though his 25,000 equals Schönhals's 32,000 less the sixth column's 7000 and his 25 per cent of 8,000 would be Schönhals's 2000 prisoners, our arithmetic); Alombert and Colin, t. IV (the French official history of 1908, which has no official French relation of the combat and rests, by its own list, on French letters, reports, the journal of Dupont's division and officers' service notes, most of them printed in Alombert's book, on two partial Austrian eyewitness relations in the Vienna war archives, on Danilewski's Russian relation, and with precautions on Talandier's narrative, those derived from it and Rozat's fragment; it sets Kotzebue aside for the fighting but uses him, with every reserve, for positions before the engagement; all these are read as t. IV prints them, not as originals); Schönhals (the Austrian account written in 1831 and printed in 1873, which by its own footnote takes some details from Kotzebue for want of more reliable sources and whose editors call it meagre and incomplete, and which by its preface draws what it says of the French army's operations from that army's bulletins, not inspected; its evening narrative follows nearly sentence for sentence the Austrian relation that t. IV quotes in translation on pp. 161-162, from the French front on the spur with two guns and about 400 cavalry to Schmidt's death, the 1000 men laying down their arms and the two guns recovered, so for the evening the two are not independent: Schönhals follows that relation or a source it shares); Moriggl (the Austrian and Tyrolean account of 1861, already registered, used only for the order of battle at the Rhine crossing, with French strengths at second hand).
